topic: The Pi-Collision Paradox: Why Bouncing Blocks Count Digits of Pi
target_audience: University students (Physics/Math) or curious high schoolers

sections.title: The Hook: A Paradoxical Counting Puzzle
sections.content: Introduce a 1D physics scenario: A small block of mass m and a large block of mass M (where M = 100^n * m) collide on a frictionless surface against a wall. The question: How many total collisions occur before the blocks stop moving toward the wall?
sections.example: Visualize two blocks, 'Tiny' and 'Huge', on a track. As the mass ratio increases (1:1, 1:100, 1:10000), the number of collisions grows surprisingly to 3, 31, 314...

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Elastic Collision & Conservation
sections.content: Briefly explain the Conservation of Momentum and Kinetic Energy. Use a vector diagram to show how velocity changes sign during a collision between two masses, setting the stage for the 'state space' representation.
sections.example: A rubber ball bouncing off a bowling ball. We represent the velocities of both blocks as coordinates (v1, v2) on a 2D plane.

sections.title: The Geometry of Collisions: The Phase Space Arc
sections.content: Introduce the 'Phase Space' concept. Show that conservation of energy forms an ellipse in this space. Collisions are represented as lines crossing the axes. The number of collisions equals the number of times the state trajectory crosses the 'boundary' lines.
sections.example: An animation showing a point bouncing off two 'walls' in a pie-slice-shaped region of the phase space, tracing a circular arc.

sections.title: The Reveal: Linking Physics to Pi
sections.content: Explain that as the mass ratio M/m grows, the angle of the pie-slice becomes smaller (specifically arcsin(sqrt(m/M))). The trajectory effectively 'unrolls' the circle. The number of hits corresponds to the digits of Pi.
sections.example: Overlay the trajectory arc onto a circle diagram. Show that for M = 1,000,000 * m, the result is exactly 3141 collisions—the first four digits of Pi.

sections.title: Summary & Synthesis
sections.content: Recap the deep connection: Discretized physics (collisions) converges to continuous geometry (Pi). Emphasize how complex dynamic systems often hide fundamental mathematical constants.
sections.example: A final visual showing the blocks colliding, then transitioning into the digits of Pi (3.14159...) appearing one by one as the collision counter increments.
